newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus parliament approves 1997 state budget.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus parliament approves 1997 state budget.

text.p: The Cyprus parliament on Wednesday approved a 1997 state budget which includes a projected rise in the deficit of 11.5 percent over the estimated figure for last year.
Net spending for 1997 was forecast at 1.689 billion Cyprus pounds ($ 3.3 billion) against revenue of 1.106 billion, yielding a deficit of 583 million pounds.
Projected spending as set out in government budgets put before parliament in 1996 was 1.545 billion pounds against revenue of 1.023, yielding a defecit of 522 million.
The 1997 budget did not include any provision for taxation increases.

It does not cover the northern third of the island, which has been occupied by Turkey since it invaded in 1974 in the wake of a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military ruling in Greece at the time.

The budget was approved late Wednesday by a majority of four parties in the 56-member House of Repesentatives. The five deputies of the socialist Edek party abstained, expressing disagreement with government economic policies.
The budget, separated into ordinary, development and spending on refugees, did not include spending on defence.
Public debt excluding intragovernmental is expected to represent 52.6 percent of the gross national product (GDP) compared with 54.1 in 1996.

GDP growth of 3.5 percent is expected compared with estimates of 2.5 percent in 1996. Last year was generally regarded as a difficult one because of a slowdown in tourism, the eastern Mediterranean island's main money spinner.
Inflation is estimated at 2.8 percent, marginally lower than 1996 estimates of 3.0 percent, while unemployment is expected to be 2.9 percent from 3.0 percent estimated in 1996.
Deputies of right wing Disy and centre-right Diko, which are partners in the government and have a majority in parliament, praised economic policies for creating conditions of "growth and stability".
Communist Akel, the largest opposition party with 19 seats in parliament, took the opportunity during the three-day debate to blast government economic and political policies.

Centre-left United Democrats leader George Vassiliou, president of Cyprus with Akel backing between 1988 and 1993, accused the government of trying to present a picture of fiscal improvement by lowering its defence spending in the first three years of its administration.

The island's finance minister, Christodoulos Christodoulou, is due to give a news conference on Thursday to respond to the opposition's charges. He has accused them of electioneering with an eye on a presidential election due in early 1998.
